Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01009

Knowledge applies to its different cases in degrees, just as existence does. These degrees differ in priority, age, strength, and weakness. Knowledge of God’s own being is knowledge in the fullest sense. It is the oldest kind of knowledge because it causes all other knowledge, and it is the clearest and most evident in itself. It seems hidden to us because it is so clear and our sight is too weak to grasp it; the very reason it is hidden from us is the reason it is most clear in itself. The same applies to knowledge of a cause compared with knowledge of its effect, and to knowledge of a substance compared with knowledge of a feature that depends on that substance. But “knowledge” as an action, a change in the knower, or a relation—such as teaching, learning, or being a knower—is a shared word used in different senses, or a figurative use.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01010
XIX. A Sign That the Soul Has a Sacred Power
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01011

Know that all knowledge comes from the holy world, but souls differ in their readiness to receive it. When the soul is fully ready, it makes no difference whether the knowledge is a first truth or a further conclusion. A person’s grasp of first truths is like the way they grasp a theoretical conclusion once they see the middle steps that prove it: in both cases, the knowledge seems to come without a cause. But nothing exists without a cause. The cause may be open and visible, or hidden from view. The one who places knowledge in ready souls is, in truth, a cause hidden from the senses: the Teacher of great strength in the highest realm. Its action in souls is very subtle. Yet it may come from within to the outward mind, as with the prophets, or appear from the hidden world in the visible world, as with the saints. The visible causes—study, repetition, and listening to a human teacher—only prepare the soul; they do not compel knowledge to appear. That is why these methods may succeed or fail.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01012

Every move from first truths to theoretical conclusions must either come through a human teacher or not. If it does, the chain must eventually reach something learned without a teacher, through the person’s own insight. Otherwise teaching and learning would continue without end. Anyone who studies a subject deeply and keeps at it will discover something that their teachers and earlier scholars did not, whether much or little. The door to the unseen world is open to everyone unless a barrier within them blocks it. As a person works and turns inward, the mind becomes finer, the natural spark grows ready, and the soul becomes like flint ready to strike a flame from the unseen realm or catch one of the lights of the world of pure intellect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01013

We have already shown that sensing particular things prepares the soul to receive universal ideas. We have also seen that when ideas fit together, the mind can judge that one belongs to another. Often, when the mind holds one idea in view, it forms the matching idea of another because it has sensed particular examples of it. The mind can then become certain that one applies to the other, without getting this knowledge from a teacher, a book, a report, or repeated testimony. So people can learn from themselves. This kind of direct insight is called intuition. People differ in how ready they are for it. Some are so slow to grasp things that they might spend a lifetime on one question and still fail to solve it. Others are the opposite: a slight turn of attention is enough for them to see the answer.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01014

Since people’s minds differ in clarity, strength, and readiness for insight, there may be a soul at the highest level: one that shines brightly with the light of the unseen world and quickly receives knowledge from the source of all good and mercy. Because it is so ready, such a person grasps many truths in a very short time, without searching for them or wanting to do so. The sharp mind moves straight to conclusions without working through the middle steps, then moves from those conclusions to others, until it reaches the furthest human questions and highest human stages. This is called a sacred power. It differs from other souls in both how much it can hold and how it understands. In quantity, it can hold more middle steps in view. In quality, it moves faster from one idea to another, from first truths to derived truths, and from starting points to final conclusions.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01015

It also grasps pure intellectual realities as they are in themselves, not only through general meanings and definitions. Reaching the realities of those intelligible things is the heart of understanding. General knowledge is still a means to reach them, once its meanings are firm and settled in the soul. That is why it has been said, “Knowledge is the seed of direct vision.” Most people first set out the question they want to answer and then search for the middle steps that prove it. The sacred soul finds the middle step first, then reaches the conclusion. That is how proofs from a cause work in reality.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01016
XX. Knowing a Cause Gives Knowledge of Its Effect, but Not the Other Way Around
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01017

The first claim is this: a cause either causes an effect by itself or does not. If it needs some added condition to have an effect, then it is not the real cause by itself. The real cause is the whole made up of it and that condition. The same question applies to that whole, until we reach something that produces its effect by its own nature. Anyone who knows this cause must know that its nature makes it the cause of that effect. If they know the cause as it is, they must know it in the very way that makes the effect follow from it. Once they know that it causes the effect, they must know the effect too, because knowing one side of a relation in the way that brings the relation about gives knowledge of the other side. This is the argument found in the books of the philosophers.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01018

I say that there are two kinds of cause. One causes its effect by its essence, as four is the cause of evenness and a triangle is the cause of having three angles. Once we know the essence of this kind of cause, we must know what follows from it, because the effect follows from the cause’s essence. The other kind does not cause its effect through its essence, but through its existence, either in the mind or in the outside world. For this kind, knowing the cause by itself does not give us knowledge of its effect. Nor does knowing that it exists in the general sense of “existing.” What produces the effect is not the essence itself or existence in general, but this particular, individual existence. Until we know that specific existence, we do not know its effect. And, as we have seen, we can know a real existence in itself only by becoming one with it or by knowing something that contains and gives rise to it. Then knowledge of its effect is the effect’s own existence, just as knowledge of the cause’s existence is the cause’s own existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01019

So if we know a cause in the way described, we must know its effect, and the effects of that effect, all the way through its chain of effects. This answers an argument by Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī. He says that if “knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect” means that knowing the cause’s essence gives knowledge of its effect, that is true only when the effect follows from the essence of its cause. If it means knowing the cause as cause and the effect as effect, that is true but not useful, since related things are known together, with neither coming before the other. And if it means knowing the cause in every respect, that is also unhelpful, since knowing a whole includes knowing its parts.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01020

If someone knows every aspect of the cause, one of those aspects is that it produces this effect. Yet the whole does not produce its part; if anything, the part helps make the whole. But the philosophers mean none of these things. They mean that knowing a cause in the real way that makes it a cause establishes that its effect must exist. The cause, with its true causal reality, stands to the necessary existence of its effect as an essence stands to what follows from that essence. Every effect follows from its cause’s essence, whether that essence is existence itself, something other than existence, or something that includes existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01021

Someone might object that the cause’s own being differs from its being a cause. The cause’s causal role is understood only in relation to its effect, while its own being is not understood in relation to anything. The First Principle, however, exists in itself and causes everything else. It would be contradictory if its being as a cause had to be understood through its effect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01022

It would also follow that the cause existed alongside its effect even though it comes before it. Since cause and causal role differ, and since the cause’s own being is not understood through the effect, knowing the cause itself need not give knowledge of the effect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01023

We answer that the cause’s role cannot be an added, positive feature on top of its essence and existence. Otherwise, that added causal role would itself need another cause, and the chain would continue without end. The cause’s role is its own specific being. But how can one thing be both a substance and a relation, when a relation is a feature? As we explained in the discussion of relations, a substance’s existence differs from its essence as the mind understands it. A substance may cause something by its own reality. When we understand its essence in that way, we do not also understand that it is a cause or stands in a relation. Its being a cause is a different intelligible aspect from the essence of the substance. Existence considered in itself is the substance’s own existence. Considered as causing or relating to something, it is the existence of that relation. This is what a relation really is, not what people suppose when they say relations do not exist in the outside world. Otherwise, statements such as “this is a cause and that is its effect” or “this is a father and that is a child” would be false.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01024
Someone may then say that the cause has a particular essence, different from the effect, and neither is part of the other. Since they are different, why can we not know one without knowing the other?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01025

Not at all. The difference between cause and effect is not like the difference between Zayd and ʿAmr, or one body and another, where we can think of either while ignoring the other. The particular existence of an effect follows from the cause’s existence. The effect’s existence relates to the cause’s existence as something that follows from an essence relates to that essence. The cause’s existence is the effect’s complete existence and perfection. Their difference is like the difference between what is stronger and what is weaker. Complete understanding must match the existence of the thing in the outside world—indeed, it must become one with it. So if a thing is the direct cause of an effect by its own nature, knowing it as a cause must directly give knowledge of the effect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01026

The second claim is that knowing an effect does not give knowledge of its particular cause. Whatever produces a thing must be its cause. If we know the cause because we know some other thing, that knowledge must itself cause our knowledge of the cause. But the effect’s existence is one with our knowledge of it, as we explained. So the effect would have to cause, in some way, our knowledge of its own cause.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01027

But if an effect, in its particular existence, follows from a particular cause, then for the effect to cause the existence of that very cause would mean that something comes before itself, which is impossible. Still, an effect is possible in itself: in its essence it is equally able either to exist or not to exist. It therefore needs something to tip the balance, some cause or other, though not necessarily a particular cause. Knowing that an effect exists in this respect gives us knowledge that some cause exists. That is why possibility makes a thing need a cause in general.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01028

Since an effect needs a cause because it is possible, knowing its essence gives knowledge of some cause in general. But the cause produces its effect through its own particular essence. If it produced an unspecified effect, it would need another condition to make the effect particular; then the true cause would be the cause together with that condition. So a particular cause, through its particular reality, produces a particular effect. Knowing the particular cause gives knowledge of that particular effect, but knowing the effect does not give knowledge of its particular cause.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01029

If an effect does not specify its particular cause, one might ask, how does it come from this cause rather than another? The particular effect requires a cause in general. But the particular cause specifies the particular effect. The effect does not choose its cause; the cause produces that effect. Since the cause, by its own nature, brings this effect into existence, no other cause can also produce it; two complete causes cannot act on the same effect at once. There are many similar examples. The broad kind “animal” applies equally to “rational” and to other distinguishing features. Animal nature by itself does not explain why one animal is human. It needs some distinguishing feature; in this case, rationality makes it human.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01030

Likewise, a kind needs some particular existence in order to exist as an individual, but its existence as Zayd comes from Zayd’s own particular being. It is not true, as some people say, that certain kinds—such as beings created without matter—bring about their own particular identity. An essence cannot cause individuation, because a thing becomes an individual through its existence, and existence is not caused by essence. Rather, particular existence makes the essence an individual, just as a particular distinguishing feature makes a broad kind into a specific kind. Knowing an individual feature gives knowledge of the kind in that particular case. Knowing a particular distinguishing feature gives knowledge of its specific kind. But knowing that a kind or species exists only tells us that some individual exists, not which one; and knowing that a broad kind exists only tells us that some distinguishing feature exists.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01031

Someone might object that if we directly know the particular existence of an effect, without an added mental picture, then this must also give us direct knowledge of the particular being of its cause. In that case, knowing the cause and knowing the effect would each give knowledge of the other.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01032

That is not so. We have seen that a cause exists more strongly than its effect. The effect’s weak and limited existence cannot contain the cause’s existence or rise to its level. In the same way, knowledge of the effect does not give us full knowledge of the cause. This is why Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī said: “The First Cause is connected to what flows from it to us, while we are connected to it only through that cause. We may therefore observe it only as far as a thing receiving what flows from it can observe its source. We must not compare its understanding of us with our understanding of it, since its understanding reaches farther, is fuller, and contains us more completely.” Anyone who thinks that the First Cause does not know particular things is far from the truth.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01033
XXI. Knowledge of an Effect Requires Knowledge of Its Cause
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01034

This question, like the one before it, can be settled only by understanding the nature of existence. Complete certainty about something requires the intellectual form to match its actual existence in the outside world. Anything that has a cause is possible in itself; otherwise, it could not depend on a cause. As we have already said, things do not cause or depend on one another through their essences. If they did, every effect would follow from an essence, the First Principle would have an essence, and knowing any essence would reveal God’s full reality and all the causes of that essence. The parts that make existence complete would then also make an essence complete, since existence would be only an abstract relation. All of this is impossible. Every effect has an essence and an existence. If we consider only its essence, we need to know its parts—its broad kind and the feature that distinguishes it within that kind—in order to understand it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01035

If instead we consider that essence as existing, then, because it is possible, it needs a cause in general. Knowledge of it in that respect must come after knowledge that some cause makes it exist. But if we consider its particular existence, that existence is formed by its particular cause. We cannot fully know its particular existence without knowing the reality of that particular cause. In its possible essence, the thing is neither existing nor necessary. In relation to its cause, it must exist and cannot change. In the same way, knowing its essence does not require us to know that its cause exists or must exist. But certain knowledge of its particular existence comes only from knowing its cause. Knowledge through the cause is then necessary and cannot change.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01036

Just as one effect cannot have two complete causes acting on it, we cannot have full knowledge of it through some other route, apart from knowledge of its cause. Otherwise, there would be two complete causes for one thing in one respect: one cause that brings the thing into existence and another that gives us knowledge of its existence. That is impossible, because our knowledge of the thing is one with the thing itself. If the thing’s existence matches our knowledge of it, the cause’s existence must also match our knowledge of the cause, because one effect has one cause. So we have shown that we can know caused things as they truly are only by knowing their causes.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01037

Someone may object that when we know a building exists, we know that it has a builder, even though the building does not cause the builder; the reverse is true. I answer that knowing the building does not, by itself, reveal who built it. It shows that the building needs a builder. That need belongs to the building itself and follows from its essence. So this is still reasoning from a cause to an effect. Knowing that one thing needs another requires knowing both sides of the relation, so the builder is known as one side of that relation. All proofs that begin from effects work in this way. Like proofs that begin from causes, they give knowledge through the relation between cause and effect. An effect is an effect in its own existence, but in its dependence and need for a cause, it shows that some cause must exist. A proof from an effect gives certainty because it shows that some cause must exist; it gives only a likely answer about which particular cause, based on a sign or feature of that cause. This is how the matter has been explained elsewhere.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01038

In general, a belief about something that we have not learned through its causes may be very strong and clear, but it can still change. Knowledge that comes from knowing the thing’s causes does not change, even if the effect itself changes. True knowledge of a thing is, in reality, one with its existence. These are among the most subtle questions in divine philosophy, understood only by those who have reached the highest level of knowledge. We will explain this further when we discuss God’s knowledge.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01039

As for something that does not depend on a cause or on parts that make it up, knowledge of it is either self-evident, impossible to attain, or possible only through evidence and effects; in that last case, we do not know its full essence. God has no proof or definition. Nothing causes Him to exist, whether as an agent or as an end; nothing makes Him up, whether matter and form or a broad kind and a distinguishing feature.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01040

Yet nothing is without Him. He is the proof of everything and closer to everything than anything else, as the Qur'an says: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein,” and “He is with you wherever you are.” He is the proof of His own being, as the Qur'an says: “God bears witness that there is no god but Him”; “Is your Lord not enough as a witness over all things?”; and “What is the greatest witness? Say: God.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01041

There is a serious problem here, especially for our view that cause and effect belong to existence itself, while essence is only derived from it. Our knowledge of ourselves is identical with our own existence, and our existence is one of the things that has a cause. We have established that knowledge of something caused comes only through knowledge of its cause. If our knowledge of ourselves is so certain, then our knowledge of the cause of our existence should be just as certain. Nothing is more certain than our knowledge of ourselves, because knowing ourselves is identical with being ourselves. Nothing can be more present to a thing than the thing is to itself. So we should know the cause of our existence with equal certainty. But the cause of our existence leads back to the Necessary Being, and we have said that only the Necessary Being can know God’s full reality. As the Qur'an says, “They do not encompass Him in knowledge,” and “All faces are humbled before the Living, the Self-Sustaining.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01042

One of those who seek God has found an answer to this problem, though words cannot fully express it because the path is so subtle and hard to see. We can still point toward it. Since knowing ourselves is identical with our own existence, the knowledge of the cause of our self-knowledge must be identical with the cause’s own existence, not with our existence. The cause’s existence is identical with the cause itself. It is present to itself, not to us. An effect’s existence depends on its cause, but it is not identical with that cause. Knowledge follows the same pattern as existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01043

So although we know ourselves through knowledge of our source, our knowledge of that source is its existence, together with its act of bringing us into being. Since the source causes us, our knowledge of it comes before our knowledge of ourselves, just as its existence comes before ours. Knowledge follows existence in strength and weakness, and in being a cause or an effect. A thing exists in itself as an effect, but it exists more fully in its source and cause. Its being with its maker is stronger than its being with itself: with itself, it exists only as something possible; with its maker, it exists as something that must be. All things exist in the First Principle in a way higher than any other way of existing. A prophetic prayer says: “O Being, O Source of being, O One who exists before every existence, after every existence, and gives existence to every existence.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01044
XXII. Knowledge Through Causes Gives Only Universal Knowledge
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01045

Know that we can know a thing either through a form that matches its essence or through its very existence. We know ourselves and the forms present to our souls in this second way. Later philosophers say that God knows things through mental forms added to His being. Any knowledge through an image or form is universal. Even if we add a thousand details to it, the idea can still apply to many things. So, if we know things through their first causes and explanations in this way, we will know all their effects, even particular individuals, only in a universal way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01046

The philosophers who defend this view, such as Avicenna and his followers Bahmanyār and others, explain it as follows. In The Healing and The Salvation, Avicenna says that the Necessary Being cannot understand things by learning them from those things. Otherwise, either the things He understands would make up His own being, or understanding them would be an added feature of His being. In the first case, His being would depend on things. In the second, He would not be necessary in every respect. He would depend on something outside Himself and would have a state that came from another thing, which would mean that another thing could affect Him. The principles we have already established rule out these possibilities.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01047

Since God is the source of all existence, He understands from Himself what He causes to exist. He is the source of complete beings directly, and of things that come to be and pass away through their kinds first, and then, through those kinds, through their individuals. He cannot know changing things as changing, by a knowledge tied to one time and one individual. He cannot know at one time that something exists and at another that it no longer exists. If each state required a separate image, neither image would remain alongside the other, and God’s being would change. On the other hand, if He knew perishable things only through their abstract essences and what follows from them, He would not know them as perishable. And if He knew them as joined to matter, its features, time, individuality, and composition, He would know them through sense or imagination, not intellect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01048

So God knows every thing in a universal way, yet no particular thing, not even a speck in the heavens or the earth, escapes His knowledge. It takes a subtle mind to understand how this can be. Here is how it works. When God knows Himself and knows that He is the source of every existent thing, He knows the first beings that come from Him and what follows from them. Every thing must be made necessary in some respect by its cause. These causes lead to one another until they bring about particular events. God therefore knows the causes and how they match their effects. He knows what must follow from them, the time between events, and their cycles. He could not know the causes without knowing these results. This lets Him know particular things through their qualities, as one kind of thing, or through their relation to a particular time or state. If we consider that state together with all its features, it too is unique. It depends on the causes that make each kind appear in its own particular individual. In this way, a particular thing can have a description that belongs to it alone.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01049

Avicenna continues: if you know all the movements of the heavens, you know every particular eclipse, conjunction, and separation that occurs. You know them in a universal way. You can say of a certain eclipse that it will happen after a certain period of motion, at a particular time, from a particular direction, and in a particular season; that the moon will move from it toward a given opposite position; and that a certain interval will separate it from a similar eclipse before or after it. You know every feature of each eclipse, yet you know it universally, because the same description could apply to many eclipses. Still, through some proof you know that this eclipse will happen only once.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01050

This does not make the knowledge any less universal, if we remember what was said earlier. That was Avicenna’s account. His view is that God knows every existing thing, including each particular, but knows each one through a set of universal qualities and relations that identify it alone. He does not mean that God knows only the kinds of things and misses their individual features. Some later philosophers, including Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi and his peers, disagreed with Avicenna about forms being established in God’s being. But they did not complete the account of knowledge either. They did not reach the explanation they wanted. We have answered their objections to Avicenna and shown where their arguments fall short. God willing, we will explain the true way God knows things later.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01051
XXIII. Knowledge of Particular Things Must Change If They Change
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01052

In The Healing, Avicenna tries to explain how particular things can be known without changing the knower. He says: if you knew an eclipse in the way it happens, or remained forever as you are, you would know not merely the general idea of an eclipse but every eclipse that occurs. Its happening and its absence would be the same to you, and would not change anything in you. In either case, your knowledge would be the same: that an eclipse with certain features occurs after another eclipse, or after the sun reaches a certain position, after a certain length of time, and so on. Your statement would be true before that eclipse, while it occurs, and after it. But if you include time in your knowledge and know at one moment that an eclipse is not happening, then at another that it is happening, your knowledge cannot remain the same. A new act of knowledge would arise in you. You could not be as you were before once the eclipse occurred. And you are a being in time and moments, while the First Being is not; it is even less fitting to describe Him as making a new judgment about something from within one time and then another.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01053

To explain: knowledge received from things, rather than from their first causes, must change when those things change. If you know Zayd is in the house while he is there, and then he leaves, either your first knowledge remains or it does not. If it remains, it is no longer knowledge; it has become error. The belief has changed in quality, from knowledge to ignorance. If it does not remain, then the change is even clearer. Some people say that knowing something will exist is the same as knowing it exists once it does. This is wrong for two reasons.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01054

First, if it were true, then if we knew today that a future night would come, we would already know it was night when that time arrived—even if we were in a place where we could not tell night from day. In the same way, if we knew the sun would rise later, we would know it had risen when it did, even if we could not see it or hear about it. But that conclusion is false, so the claim that leads to it is false. Second, knowledge must match what is known. “This will exist” differs from “this exists now.” The first means that something absent now will exist later. Since these two states differ and cannot hold at once, the images in the mind must differ too. Knowledge taken from changing things must change with them. Knowledge that comes from a higher source and another beginning does not follow its object in this way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01055

Al-Tusi writes in his commentary on the treatise on knowledge that many things may differ either in their natures or in number while sharing one nature. Things that share a nature may either fail to exist together or exist together. The first kind must exist with or in time; the second must exist in or with space. Time is the first cause of change, because it continually passes and changes what exists in it or alongside it. Space is the first cause of plurality among things that exist together. This means that their parts have an order and stand in different positions: one part is in a certain direction or at a certain distance from another. Anything with this kind of arrangement is material.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01056

When universal natures exist as many individuals, their first causes of individuality and distinction are time, as with movements; space, as with bodies; or both, as with changing individuals. A nature that is not in time or space is not tied to either. We do not ask when or where humanity exists by itself, or when five is half of ten. But once we mean this human being, or these particular fives and tens, their individuality may tie them to a time or place. Even different kinds of things, such as the heavenly bodies and the universal kinds of earthly elements, can still be tied to time and space.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01057

With this in mind, we can return to the question. If something is perceived as belonging to a time or place, it is perceived only through a bodily tool, such as an outer or inner sense. Such a tool perceives changes that are present in its own time and judges them to exist. It misses what belongs to another time and judges it absent, saying it was or will be but is not now. It perceives separate things that can be pointed out and judges where they are and how far away they are. But a perceiver that is not limited in this way would perceive fully. It would know which event occurs in every time, how long it lasts, and how much time lies between it and any earlier or later event. It would not judge anything absent; it would know that each thing exists in its own time and not at other times. It would know where every individual exists and how it relates to every other thing in every direction, including the distances between them. It would know all of this as it truly is, without judging things to be here or there, present or absent, now existing or not existing. Such a knower is not in time or space, so all times and places are equally present to it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01058

Only a being that exists in a certain time and place is limited to saying “now,” “here,” “present,” “absent,” “in front of me,” or “behind me.” A being that knows everything knows all things most fully. It does not judge some things absent, but knows every thing in the “clear book” of existence: what has passed, what is present, what will come, and whatever else can be said of things. That is how a timeless knower knows particulars in a universal way. The image is like a rolled-up scroll. A reader looks at one letter after another and loses sight of what came before or what comes later. The person holding the whole scroll sees all its letters at once, with the same relation to each one. This kind of knowledge cannot belong to a being in time or space. It needs no bodily tool or separate image. Nothing, universal or particular, can escape it. Not even a leaf falls without its knowing.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01059

Particular knowledge in the narrower sense—knowing something through a bodily tool, at a certain time and place—belongs only to a bodily perceiver. So saying that God does not know particulars in this bodily way does not diminish Him. It only confirms that He has no bodily senses. Such knowledge would change His being and His essential attributes. It changes only what is known and the relations between Him and those things.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01060

I see several problems with this account. First, as we have explained, bodily matter is a source of absence and ignorance. Prime matter, as it is in itself, has no image that matches it in reality. The same is true of absences, possibilities, and other weak or unfinished kinds of existence. If we try to understand prime matter as it is, we cannot—not because our intellect is weak, but because prime matter itself has no form in existence, only a capacity to receive forms. The capacity for a form is not the form. This applies to material bodies and to things that have position and shape as well.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01061

Second, philosophers have argued that something cannot be understood as a sensible thing except through a bodily tool. Their argument is conclusive. Third, the way a thing exists in reality does not change depending on who perceives it. A material thing is always material in itself. A thing that changes in itself always changes. The reality of space and spatial things is that each part is separate from the others and does not exist together with them. This does not change for different perceivers. Even if the eye were as large as the greatest sphere, the difference between near and far would remain.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01062

The same applies to time and timed things: each part of time makes the others absent, so no two parts can exist together. We have shown that all substantial forms in matter, whether heavenly or earthly, have changing existence and come into being anew at each moment. How can an existence that changes in its very nature be fixed, eternal, and unchanging for some other knower?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01063

Fourth, knowledge of things must come either from the things themselves, be identical with those things, or come from their causes in a cause-and-effect order. If knowledge comes from the things themselves, it must change when they change. If it is identical with the things, the change is even clearer. If it comes from causes, this can mean two things. One: the causes are known through separate intellectual forms, as the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, including Avicenna, usually say. Those universal forms are arranged by universal causes and lead to universal results. They may include particulars in a universal way, but they do not tell us about each individual as an individual. Even a thousand added details cannot make an image-based idea apply to only one thing. The other possibility is that knowledge is the existence of the things themselves. This is the fullest kind of knowledge. Through it, all things—universals and particulars, their natures and their individuals, with all their features and states—are known as they are. But this account depends on understanding the simple intellect of the Necessary Being and the separate luminous intellects, which contain lower things in a higher way. These are keys to the unseen world. Through this kind of knowledge, every existent thing, even a lifeless object, is alive.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01064

Fifth, for this philosopher, knowledge is not a relation alone. He defines it as the form of a thing being present in the soul. A form present in matter is not any of the four kinds of perception he recognizes—sensation, imagination, estimation, or intellection—because each requires some degree of separation from matter. A form embedded in matter is not free of matter, much less free of the features and relations that come with it. If such a material form were directly perceived as it exists in matter, there would have to be a fifth kind of perception, although perception has already been limited to those four.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01065

This confirms what I have argued: merely being related to something that exists does not, by itself, amount to intellectual knowledge. Avicenna makes the same point in The Healing when explaining God's knowledge. He warns us not to think that God's intellectual relation to things is a relation to them in whatever state they happen to exist. If it were, every cause that produces a form in matter would itself be an intellect, simply because that form could be made an object of thought by separating it from matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01066

For an intellectual relation, the object must be present as something that can be understood. If God's knowledge depended on things as they exist outside Him, He would know only what exists at a given moment. He could not know a thing before it came to exist. Nor could He know Himself as the ordered source of that thing until He actually brought it about. Yet God's own nature is such that every existence can proceed from Him. Knowing Himself as that source therefore includes knowing what can proceed from Him, whether or not it yet exists outside Him. The divine world of knowledge embraces both actual and possible beings.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01067

That is the end of Avicenna's argument. The point is that the existence of an object and a knower, taken separately, is not enough for intellectual knowledge of the object. The object must be present in a form that can be understood. It must have a way of existing as something known, not merely a material existence outside the knower. Forms that are separate from matter can have this kind of existence. Material things, considered only in their material existence, cannot enter an intellectual relation in that same way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01068
XXIV. Explaining the Different Meanings of “Intellect”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01069

Know that, as we will explain in the Book of the Soul, the human soul has two powers: one for knowing and one for action. These two powers cannot be separated from each other, unlike the powers in other animals. As for the power of action, human acts can be good or bad. We may know that something is good or bad without learning it through reasoning, or we may need to reason it out. Reasoning it out requires fitting premises. Three things are involved: a power that distinguishes good from bad; the premises used to work out what is good or bad; and the actions themselves, which are called good or bad.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01070

The word “intellect” is used for all three, but in different senses. First, it can mean the power that distinguishes good from bad. Most people mean this when they say that someone is intelligent. They might say that Muʿāwiya was intelligent, though some would refuse to call him so and say an intelligent person must be religious. In this use, “intelligent” means wise and good at working out what good to do and what evil to avoid.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01071

Second, speakers may say “reason requires this,” “reason rejects that,” or “reason accepts or refuses this.” Here, they mean what most people accept at first glance: ideas or opinions accepted by all or most people, and judgments people commonly praise.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01072

Third, ethics books use “intellect” to mean sticking to tested and familiar actions over a long time, until those actions form a habit or character. This sense relates to the conclusions reached by practical reason as the starting ideas of thought relate to the theoretical intellect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01073

As for the knowing power—the “intellect” discussed in the Book of the Soul—the philosophers use the word either for the power itself or for what it understands. What it understands may be an idea or a judgment that the soul has from birth, or something it learns. Sometimes “intellect” means only the knowledge gained through learning.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01074

The power itself can receive knowledge of the realities of things. It is either empty of every form or not. If empty, but able to receive forms, it is like prime matter: it has only the power and readiness to receive forms and has not yet become any one of them. In that state it is called the potential or material intellect. If it is not empty, then it either contains only first principles, or it also contains conclusions reached through thought.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01075

If it contains only first principles, which are tools for gaining further knowledge, it is called the intellect in habit. It has the ability and habit of reaching conclusions and can move toward the intellect in act. It is not yet the intellect in act, because no actual intellectual existence has yet been formed. First principles and general ideas alone do not make a thing fully actual; an indefinite, common idea must become a specific thing. In the world of thought, first principles relate to detailed intellectual forms as the general idea of a body relates to particular kinds of physical thing. A physical thing does not exist outside the mind through the idea of body alone; it must become a particular thing with its own nature. In the same way, the intellect does not become actual through the general idea of existence, thinghood, or simple principles such as “one is half of two” and “the whole is greater than one of its parts.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01076

If the soul at this level has many first principles, strong readiness, and quickly receives intellectual light, it may be like a wick that is so full of heat it almost lights itself. This is called the sacred power, as in the verse, “Its oil would almost shine even if no fire touched it.” Otherwise, it remains the intellect in habit. If it has also gained theoretical conclusions, these are either not present to it now but can be brought to mind as soon as it turns its attention to them, or they are present and clearly in view. In the first case it is called the intellect in act; in the second, the acquired intellect. At this level, if it sees these forms in the source from which they flow, it is called the Active Intellect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01077

People argue about whether “intellect” means the soul at one of these levels, the level itself, or the forms present in the soul. This argument is not very useful, since intellect, knower, and known are one in each of these levels. Farabi says that earlier philosophers used “theoretical intellect” in four ways: potential, actual, acquired, and active. They did not count the intellect in habit because it is not much different from potential intellect in its degree of actuality. Both are still potential, though one is closer to being actual.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01078

The potential intellect is either the soul itself, a part of it, or one of its powers, ready to draw out the essences or forms of all existing things, without their matter. It can make all these forms into its own form or forms. The forms drawn out of matter are called intelligibles when they become forms in this knowing power. They receive their name from the power that knows them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01079

This power is like matter that receives forms. Imagine wax that receives an engraved figure or shape across its whole surface and depth, until the whole piece of wax becomes that shape. This helps us understand how forms become present to the power that resembles matter and a subject for those forms. It differs from physical matter because physical matter receives figures only on its surface, not throughout its depth. Yet this knowing power does not remain separate from the forms, with its own essence set apart from them. It becomes those forms themselves. Imagine a shape pressed into wax so that it extends through its length, width, and depth. The wax then becomes that shape. This is how we should understand forms becoming present to the power that Aristotle calls the potential intellect. While the forms of things are not in it, it is intellect only in potentiality. When they appear in it in this way, it becomes intellect in act.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01080

Before they are drawn out of matter, the forms are intelligible only in potentiality. Once they are drawn out, they become forms of this knowing power. They become intellect in act because they are now intelligible in act. Being an actual intelligible and being actual intellect are one and the same. To say that the power knows in act means nothing other than that the intelligibles have become its forms and it has become those forms.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01081

Before they become intelligible in act, the forms themselves may have other features: they may be somewhere, have a position, be a quantity, have bodily qualities, act, or be acted upon. These features can belong to them one at a time or in different subjects. Once they become intelligible in act, many of those features fall away and their existence changes. The intellect may understand the meaning of “where” without itself being somewhere, or the features that make one place more specific than another.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01082

Once the forms become intelligible in act, they are counted among the things that exist, and all existing things can be understood and become forms of this power. So actual intelligibles are also actual intellect. They can be understood too. The thing understood is the same as the intellect that understands it, but in a different respect. One form can make the power actual in relation to itself, while the power remains only potential in relation to another form not yet present. Once that second form appears, the intellect becomes actual through both forms. If it becomes actual through all intelligibles and is itself one of the things understood, then when it understands itself it understands nothing outside itself.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01083

If some things are forms that have never been in matter, the intellect does not need to draw them out of matter. It finds them already separate and understands them. Their existence as understood forms is the same as their existence in themselves before anyone understands them. The same applies to what has become intellect in act in us: its actual intellect consists in the intelligible forms present in it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01084

These separate forms can be understood fully only after most or all other forms have been understood and the acquired intellect has arisen. At that point, all those forms become forms of the acquired intellect. The acquired intellect is like the matter or subject that receives them; the intellect in act is like the form of the acquired intellect. The intellect in act is in turn like the subject and matter of the acquired intellect. It is the form of the potential intellect. In this way, forms begin to descend toward bodily forms in matter. Before that, they rise, step by step, away from matter in different degrees, ordered by their level of completeness. The most complete form gives form to what is less complete, until we reach the acquired intellect. From there, forms continue downward to the potential intellect, the other soul powers, and nature.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01085

This is the end of Farabi’s account. It clearly supports the view that the knower becomes one with what it understands. It also says that a person can become a simple intellect that gathers all intelligibles within it. Given such direct statements by Farabi, by the author of The Theology of Aristotle, attributed to Aristotle, and by Porphyry, whom Avicenna says wrote a book on intellect and intelligibles and defended their union with the Active Intellect, how can later thinkers reject this honored teaching without first understanding it? Anyone who has not reached it should follow the advice Avicenna gives at the end of The Pointers.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01086
XXV. Alexander’s Account of the Intellect, Following Aristotle
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01087

In his treatise, Alexander says that Aristotle described three kinds of intellect. First is the potential intellect. By “potential,” I mean a subject that can become something through receiving a form. Prime matter is potential because it can become any kind of thing. In the same way, the intellect that has not yet understood anything is potential. It has not yet become one of the things it can understand, but it can become all of them. The power in the soul that is like this is called the potential intellect. It is not yet any existing thing in act, but it can become able to understand all existing things by receiving their forms.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01088

The universal perceiver must not already be one of the things it can perceive. Otherwise, when it tried to understand things outside itself, its own form would get in the way and block them. The senses show this. The eye has no particular color of its own, so it can see colors; the air used for smell has no smell of its own, so it can receive scents. Touch does not sense heat, cold, softness, or roughness by being exactly like the thing it senses. If it were itself a natural body, it could not be free of all the qualities it perceives. This does not mean it is free of every bodily quality, only that it is free of the particular things it perceives. It could not perceive them if it already had them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01089

The intellect, too, must not be one of the things it distinguishes. It can understand all things because it can become all things it understands. So it is not any existing thing in act; it is all things in potentiality. This is what “potential intellect” means. The senses are bodily powers and are acted upon. Each sense perceives only a limited range of things. The intellect, however, does not understand through a body or as a power belonging to a body, and it is not acted upon in the same way. It is not any existing thing in act or a particular thing that can be pointed to. It is a receptive power for forms and intelligibles. This is the potential intellect found in every human being with a complete soul.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01090

The second kind is the intellect that has begun to understand and has the ability to understand more. It can take the forms of intelligibles into itself. It is like a person who has learned a craft and can now use it on their own. The first intellect is not like a trained craftsperson; it is like someone who has only the ability to learn the craft.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01091

The third kind is the Active Intellect, which is different from the first two. It makes the potential intellect an intellect in act by giving it the habit of understanding. Aristotle compares it to light: just as light makes colors visible in act, the Active Intellect makes the potential intellect actual by giving it the power to understand. By its nature, the Active Intellect is intelligible in act because it produces acts of understanding. It is also an intellect, since the forms that are in matter become intelligible in act when the intellect separates them from matter. Once each form is understood, it becomes both actual intelligible and actual intellect. Before that, it was neither by nature.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01092

The Active Intellect may govern what happens in this world on its own, returning things to their higher, immaterial principles. Or it may do so through the motions of the heavenly bodies. Or nature may act through both the intellect and those motions. It may seem that the Active Intellect should not govern lowly things, as some people who deny the unseen world have thought. But there is no reason to think these actions beneath it. Everything it does is wise and well ordered. In general, there is an intellect and care guiding what happens here, just as the other intellects complete the souls of the heavenly bodies. Whether our souls can understand through this intellect, and whether it is present in us from the start or acquired, is another question. But the soul does not receive it as a place receives an object. The soul changes into the intelligibles, as matter changes into forms. The sense power also becomes one with the sensible forms.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01093

This is the end of Alexander’s treatise. I have quoted it to strengthen the case that the soul can become one with the Active Intellect and with the intelligibles. Since this point is very subtle and difficult, it needs more explanation. Perhaps those ready to seek it will find a way to reach it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01094
XXVI. Answering a Difficulty About the Potential Intellect Becoming Actual
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01095

You may see two problems with saying that the potential intellect becomes intellect in act. First, as we said earlier, this seems to mean that one reality changes into another. The human soul is a natural form belonging to a body. Together with the body, it makes one natural kind: the human being. How, then, can it become an intellectual substance and an intelligible form, separate from matter and bodies? We have already pointed to the answer: a thing’s existence is not the same as its essence. Existence can grow stronger. Through a continuous process, a thing can move from one kind of existence toward another. This is like black becoming deeper, or heat becoming stronger.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01096

Second, philosophers say that a body is made of two substances: matter and form. A body has an extended form, but it also has the potential to receive other forms. One simple thing cannot be actual in one respect and potential in another at the same time. So a body must be made of two parts: one that is potential and one that is actual. Philosophers also argue that the human soul survives death. If it could be destroyed, it would have both the potential to be destroyed and the actual state of remaining alive. Anything that can be destroyed can also continue to exist, so the soul would have to be made of a potential part and an actual part. This is impossible, because the soul is simple and not made of outer matter and form. If that is so, how can the soul be matter for an intellectual form?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01097

We answer that composition is required only when something is potential and actual with respect to the same perfection, or with respect to different perfections at the same level, whether sensory or intellectual. A body’s physical form is actual in one respect, while its potential to move is another respect. The soul’s existence as a natural form can be actual, while it is potential to become an intellectual form. These two sides do not require two separate subjects. The soul’s being the highest form in the natural world does not conflict with its being the first matter of the world of intellectual forms. It is the bridge between them. No natural thing becomes intellect until it has passed through the lower levels of physical matter, plant life, and animal life.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01098

We have already said that abstracting a sensible form to make it intelligible does not mean deleting some features and keeping others. It means moving from material existence to intellectual existence, by first moving through sense and imagination. The same is true of the soul. The sensing soul is the first level of animal life, after it has passed through the levels of elements, lifeless matter, and plants. At first, it senses in act but only imagines in potentiality, as with certain simple animals that have no imagination, such as worms, snails, and shellfish. Once imagination develops, the soul imagines in act and understands only in potentiality. This potential intellect can both understand and be understood only in potentiality. When the soul takes on intellectual forms, it becomes both knower and known in act. Its existence then becomes a new kind of existence, beyond the natural world and part of the intellectual world. The earlier levels belonged to the natural world or to the world between nature and intellect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01099
XXVII. How the Potential Intellect Becomes Actual Intellect
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01100

In The Origin and Return, Avicenna explains how the potential intellect becomes intellect in act, even though in his other books he rejects the idea that the intellect becomes one with what it understands. He says that when a form free of matter and its features becomes one with the intellect, it makes the intellect actual by being present in it. It does not remain separate from the intellect as a body's form is separate from its matter. If the intellect were separate from the form and understood it, then it would need another inner form in order to understand it. The same question would arise about that second form, and the chain would never end.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01101

He then asks whether the intellect in act is the form itself, the potential intellect that receives the form, or both together. The potential intellect cannot become actual simply because the form is present. Either it understands the form or it does not. If it does not, it remains potential. If it does, then it must understand the form either by gaining another form or simply because this form is present in it. If it needs another form, the chain never ends. If the form is understood simply because it is present, then either the mere presence of a form is enough, or it must be present to something capable of understanding.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01102

If mere presence is enough, then matter and the bodily features joined to forms would also be intellects, since forms are present in them. Natural forms exist in real things, mixed with other things rather than separated from them. But what is mixed with something else is not the same as what is pure and unrestricted. If, instead, the form must be present to something capable of understanding, then we have only said that it is present to something able to receive it. That restates the claim without explaining what makes it understood. So understanding is neither the form's bare presence in the potential intellect nor a separate image taken from it. The intellect in act is not simply the potential intellect as a receiver of the form.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01103

Nor can the intellect in act be the form alone while the potential intellect remains a separate subject that receives it. In that case, the intellect in potentiality would be a subject, not an intellect in potentiality. The form would be actual intellect by itself, and could not also be potential intellect. Nor can the actual intellect be the two together, the receiver and the form. Suppose it understands something outside itself. It would then need an image of that thing inside itself, and that image would be another form. It would not be the very form whose nature we are trying to explain. But the form under discussion is supposed to be the first one that makes the potential intellect actual. The same difficulty returns if we say that the intellect understands itself through parts: a part like matter, a part like form, or both. Each part would have to understand itself through one or both of those parts.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01104

Each option fails. If the part like matter understands itself, the part like form does no work. If the part like matter understands itself through the form-like part, then the form becomes the receptive, potential part and matter becomes the active form—the reverse of what was required. If the matter-like part understands itself through both parts, its form would be more than itself, which is impossible. The same reasoning applies to the part like form, and to the claim that each part understands every other part.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01105

The three options are therefore ruled out. An intellectual form relates to the potential intellect differently from the way a natural form relates to physical matter. When an intellectual form is present in the potential intellect, the two become one. The receiver and what it receives are no longer separate in their being. The actual intellect, in the full sense, is the abstract form itself. If a form makes another thing an intellect by being present in it, then, when the form exists by itself, it is even more fully an intellect. Heat makes a body hot, so heat by itself would be even more able to heat; whiteness makes a body bright to sight, so whiteness by itself would be even more visible. The form does not need another intellect to understand it. The potential intellect already knows itself as a power able to understand other things. This shows that every essence free of matter and its features is intelligible and intellect in act by itself.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01106

I suspect that Avicenna argued this way to make room for the view held by Aristotle’s followers, rather than because it was the account he himself would have given. Otherwise, he would have had to answer several objections to ideas he and other philosophers defend. The first is that we can choose the first option: the potential intellect itself becomes actual when the abstract form is present, just as the sense power becomes actual when a sensible form is present. Avicenna asks whether the form is understood because it is present in the intellect in any way, or because it is present in something capable of understanding.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01107

The right answer is the latter: it is understood because it is present in a being that can understand. We are not trying to define or explain the cause of how an abstract form is understood, so this does not make a thing explain itself. The point is that an intelligible form exists in the potential intellect differently from the way a natural form exists in matter. Matter cannot understand, and forms mixed with bodily features cannot be understood as they are. But abstract forms can be understood by the potential intellect because it can receive them. Another way to put it is that the potential intellect understands an abstract form because it is present as something without position to a being that also has no position.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01108

Second, the potential intellect is the human rational soul. If it becomes the intelligible form in act, it seems that the human being changes into a separate intellect. Avicenna rejects this kind of change between substances, especially when neither substance is material. But the soul’s existence can grow stronger, as we have explained in our discussions of potentiality and change.
